sections.title: Interoperability Test Bed

summary.text: Introduces the Interoperability Test Bed, a European Commission DIGIT service for conformance testing of IT systems through scenario-based test cases written in the GITB Test Description Language (TDL), whose steps use built-in capabilities or orchestrate extension services. Test cases typically exchange and validate messages with a system under test, and may include control flow, user interaction and data processing; the Test Bed also offers a user interface, a REST API and webhooks. DIGIT runs a shared instance and publishes all components as Docker images for local use. The section opens with build, quality, licence, documentation and Docker badges.

sections.title: About this repository

summary.text: Says the repository holds the Test Bed's two main application components: the test engine, which executes test cases and reports progress and outcome (Docker image gitb-srv), and the frontend, which provides the user interface and test, user and configuration management (gitb-ui). It notes that the simplest way to use the Test Bed is through the published Docker images and the installation guide, with building from source as the alternative.

sections.extract: This repository contains the main application components that are used by the Interoperability Test Bed. These are: The test engine, responsible for executing test cases and reporting their progress and outcome. In terms of Docker images, this component represents the `gitb-srv` image. sections.title: Technology stack

summary.text: States that gitb-srv and gitb-ui are both Java-based: gitb-srv is a Spring Boot application using Akka internally, gitb-ui is written in Scala on the Play Framework, and gitb-ui's frontend is an Angular TypeScript app built with Angular CLI.

sections.extract: Both `gitb-srv and gitb-ui are Java-based applications. Specifically, gitb-srv` is packaged as a Spring Boot application using Akka as its primary internal framework, whereas `gitb-ui` is developed in Scala and uses the Play Framework. The frontend of the `gitb-ui` component is an Angular app developed in TypeScript, and is managed in terms of scaffolding and build using Angular CLI.

sections.title: Configuration properties

summary.text: Notes that the main configuration file is gitb-ui's application.conf, which never needs direct editing because every property can be set through environment variables, via Docker or the IDE; the full list of properties is documented in the production installation guide.

sections.extract: The main configuration file of interest is `application.conf from gitb-ui` although this never needs to be adapted directly. All properties can be set through environment variables, provided either via Docker or through the IDE used for development. The full listing and documentation of properties is available here.

sections.title: Frontend (gitb-ui)

summary.text: Gives the development steps for gitb-ui: sbt compile, a run configuration for sbt run, and environment variables as needed (e.g. THEME = ec), then npm install in gitb-ui/ui before choosing one of two ways to work on the Angular app. When developing with EU Login, SESSION_SECURE must be false and SESSION_COOKIE_NAME ITB_SESSION, or session cookies are never served over HTTP and authentication loops; testing over HTTPS through a local SSL proxy is the alternative.

sections.extract: To build and run the `gitb-ui` component carry out the following steps: 1. From the `gitb-ui folder issue sbt compile`. 2. Define in your IDE a run configuration as a sbt application to run `sbt run`. 3. Set environment variables as needed. For example set `THEME = ec` for a EC-themed UI. The next step is to choose how to build and run the Angular UI application. Its resources are defined in the `gitb-ui/ui` folder

sections.title: Option 1: Work on Angular UI through Play application

summary.text: Describes the first way to develop the Angular UI: build it with npm run build (or npm run build:dev to rebuild on change) into the Play application's assets and reach it through the Play welcome page at localhost:9000, refreshing the browser after rebuilds. This mirrors production and is needed to test interactions with the Play application, such as EU Login and the various login options.

sections.extract: Using this approach you build the Angular app using Angular CLI but access it through the Play application. To do this: 1. From `gitb-ui/ui issue npm run build. This will build the app and copy it under the Play application's assets` folder. To rebuild automatically for any changes use `npm run build:dev`. 2. Access the application by first going to the Play application's welcome page at http://localhost:9000. Once

sections.title: Option 2: Work on Angular UI standalone

summary.text: Describes the second way to develop the Angular UI: run npm run build once for static resources, then npm start to serve the app at localhost:4200 with automatic reload, using the Play application only through its proxied REST API. It is the most efficient approach but cannot test Play interactions such as EU Login, although it can be used after authenticating through Play since cookies are shared.

sections.extract: Using this approach you build and serve the Angular app using Angular CLI. In this scenario the Play application is only used through its REST API which the Angular app proxies and uses. To use this approach: Only once from `gitb-ui/ui issue npm run build`. This is needed to put in place static resources used by the Angular app (most notably tinymce styles). From `gitb-ui/ui issue npm start`. This reloads the app

sections.title: Build for deployment

summary.text: Heading that introduces building the components as a Dockerised service, by one of two approaches: with the project's development tools, or with Docker Compose as a containerised build.

sections.extract: Follow these steps to build the components for deployment as a Dockerised service. Two approaches are available: Build using the project's development tools. Build using Docker Compose (containerised build).

sections.title: Build using development tools

summary.text: Says building with the development tools suits a repository already set up for development: it is faster but requires Java, Maven, NPM, SBT and Scala to be installed and the Docker images to be built by hand.

sections.extract: This approach is more suitable is you have set up the repository for development and have installed all necessary tooling. Producing build artefacts is faster but expects the necessary tools (Java, Maven, NPM, SBT, Scala) to be installed, and manual steps to build Docker images.

sections.title: Test engine (gitb-srv)

summary.text: Gives the deployment build steps for gitb-srv: run mvn clean install -DskipTests=true -Denv=docker from the root, copy gitb-testbed-service/target/itbsrv.war to a separate folder, and build the isaitb/gitb-srv image there with the Dockerfile from etc/docker/gitb-srv.

sections.extract: 1. From the current (root) folder issue `mvn clean install -DskipTests=true -Denv=docker` 2. Copy file `gitb-testbed-service/target/itbsrv.war` to a separate folder to build its Docker image. 3. Use Dockerfile `etc/docker/gitb-srv/Dockerfile from the same folder to build the image with docker build -t isaitb/gitb-srv .`.

sections.title: Create the overall service

summary.text: Explains how to assemble the service from locally built images: follow the development installation guide, create or download a docker-compose.yml that uses those images, and start it with docker compose up -d.

sections.extract: 1. Follow the development installation guide. 2. Create or download your docker-compose.yml file making use of the locally built images (see previous steps). 3. Launch the service from the folder containing your docker-compose.yml file with docker compose up -d.

sections.title: Build using Docker Compose

summary.text: Describes the containerised build with Docker Compose 2.0.0 or later, which builds all images from source with no developer tools but is slower. Six variables must be set first, and some are embedded in the images as build arguments: MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD, MYSQL_PASSWORD, DB_DEFAULT_PASSWORD (which must match MYSQL_PASSWORD), APPLICATION_SECRET, MASTER_PASSWORD and HMAC_KEY (shared by gitb-ui and gitb-srv). It gives example settings for Linux/macOS and PowerShell or a .env file, then docker compose up -d --build. These images are for development, and the published images still support runtime secrets via environment variables and _FILE variants.

sections.extract: This approach is more suitable for a containerised build, avoiding any manual steps and developer tool installations (apart from Docker Compose). Make sure that your Docker Compose is at least at version 2.0.0. Note that the overall build time in this case is slower compared to building with the relevant tools. When using this approach the images are built directly from the repository's sources using the definitions

sections.title: Using the application

summary.text: Explains first access to a running Test Bed: go to localhost:9000, click login and authenticate as admin@itb with a one-time password, refreshed at each start-up until the first login, that is printed in the gitb-ui container logs (an example log excerpt is shown). The user guide and sample tutorials cover what comes next.

sections.extract: Once a complete Test Bed instance has been set up, either in development or as a Dockerised service, access using the default Test Bed administrator account as follows: 1. Go to http://localhost:9000. 2. Click on the login button. 3. Authenticate using admin@itb. This account is set with a one-time password that is refreshed at start-up until a first login is made. sections.title: Contact

summary.text: Invites feedback and questions about the GITB Test Bed software as issues in the repository, or by email to the Test Bed team at DIGIT-ITB@ec.europa.eu.

sections.extract: For feedback or questions regarding the GITB Test Bed software you are invited to post issues in the current repository. In addition, feel free to contact the Test Bed team via email at DIGIT-ITB@ec.europa.eu.

sections.title: See also

summary.text: Refers readers to the Interoperable Europe Portal site for general information on the Test Bed and GITB, and, for standalone data validation rather than a full conformance testing platform, to the Test Bed's separate XML, RDF (SHACL), JSON and CSV validators.

sections.extract: For general information on all aspects of the Interoperability Test Bed and the GITB software in particular you may refer to its Interoperable Europe Portal site. The GITB software is used to realise a complete conformance testing platform. If you are more interested in standalone data validation you may find interesting the Test Bed's validators for XML, RDF, JSON and CSV content.
